instruction.what: Step 2.1, the structure of one subgroup (stage 1, B3): what stands with the subgroup's words in each verse, read from the stored structure. One item at a time: double-meaning (a surface with more than one code), qualifier (negators and the word each reaches, adjectives, adverbs, prepositional qualifiers), entity (who is named or referred to), direction (from whom to whom, by the grammar), pairing (one row for each partner collection: its words in the verses shared with the subgroup). Nothing here says what anything does for the inner being; that begins at step 3.1.
read: Take one row at a time (`rows`): what it asks, its occurrences (`as`: member, the subgroup's word; partner, the other word), and its verses.

Read each verse (`verses`) from its stored structure, one line for each word: * marks an occurrence of the subgroup; then the position, surface, Strong's code and morph, and what the pairing makes of the word (its type, the qualifier it carries, a negator, a party, the collections of a word of another collection). Nothing is evaluated that is not stored.
Where each word stands: its side and distance from the subgroup's word, from the positions. Adjacency is not scope: a negator or qualifier is read for the word it reaches by the grammar.
A pairing row shows the WordNet control for its partner collection: a pairing WordNet gives and the verses do not show is one to look for; a pairing only the verses show has no control.
Differences in meaning are read from the base data (the Strong's code, the morph, the construction), not from the English alone. The subgroup's 1.1 senses (`senses`) are what the findings build on.
write: Fill `answer.rows`: for each row, disposition observed with its `findings`, or none with its `reason` (where the row allows none: nothing of the item stands with the subgroup in its verses).

One finding for each distinct thing the structure shows; the same finding in several verses is ONE finding naming all its occurrences; a verse that shows something different is its own finding. Together the findings name every occurrence of the row (occurrence ids or verse references), each in one finding.

kind: as the template gives it (pairing; relation for direction; face for double-meaning). obs_text: concise; names the verses it holds in, as the package writes the references (for example Act 18:4); states what the structure shows (which word, where it stands, what it reaches or gives by the grammar); never a verse restated, never what it does for the inner being.
basis: stated (the verse says it) or read (read from the structure), with `grounds`: words copied exactly from the verses it is tied to (the record checks them).
Each subgroup's surface has its own finding; none joins two subgroups. A data error is named in grounds, not fixed.

`older`: answer each older observation shown under the row, once: keep (with `nature`), restate (with `nature`, `new_text`, `checked`), merge (with `into`), consume (with `carriers` ["this"] or observation ids, and `mapping`), delete_neither (with `reason`), carry (with `to` and `reason`), defer (with `collection`, `nature`, `finding`). One listed under another row is answered there.
Then: Collection-Build.ps1 -Action RecordStructure -File <the answer file> (-Check to preview). The record refuses the whole file on any fault and lists every fault.

keep.text: Morph is read, not carried: where occurrences of a word show different stems or voices, record whether the subject does, undergoes or causes the act.

A word that is only a homonym or a name, with no meaningful context, is recorded as such (tag no-human-context) and left. Data errors found while reading are flagged (tag data-error), not fixed in the reading.

A word is read per its lettered Strong's code (its grain), never the bare lemma (B:113). The occurrences of a word with several senses are related per grain and never aggregated across grains: related verses are same-grain occurrences.
One observation per finding, never a duplicate description; a finding applying to several verses or words carries several nodes, each with the word's role in it.
One observation per finding: the same description is never written twice. Applied to another verse, word or scope it gains a node on the existing observation.
Observation text is concise and tied to this verse's content, never a restatement of the word's dictionary sense. A transliteration is never given without its gloss.
Where the evidence points to more than one reading, each is its own observation with its own evidence.
A re-read includes the observations already recorded for the verse, so the reading sees prior findings and builds on them.
Missing data in the base extract is named as a gap, never substituted from memory or outside knowledge.

Every older live observation with a live node on an occurrence of the row (a stage that is not the build's own) is answered in fill.older when the row is recorded, once: keep or restate (each with its marker), merge into a named observation, consume (live observations carry its meaning, stated in words, verified before it is deleted), delete as neither (comment first), or defer to a named collection (marked now; only the finding is left to that collection). An observation already marked by the validation, answered in a build or deferred is not asked again. A new observation whose text equals that of another live observation of the collection is refused, the other named. LayerCheck re-derives both from the tables. The end state of a collection's build is that every observation of its scope is marked and fixed or deleted, every word node complete or with its reason, and each deferral owned by a named collection.

When a verse is worked, every existing observation and node on it, of any stage, is checked against the verse by its wording. The stage is not an indication of the nature of an observation and is never used to filter. Each observation is accepted, modified (changed in place; the old value, the new value and the reason are kept in ib_observation_change), soft deleted (the `deleted` column, with the reason), merged (a duplicate description, into the observation that is kept) or, when its wording shows it is not verse understanding, left exactly as it is with the reason. The check's fixes are part of it and need no separate approval. Nothing is physically deleted.

The nodes of a layer observation are the occurrences the aspect demands (a word's occurrences, the group's occurrences, the partner's occurrences in the verses they share), written by the recorder with the collection and the subgroup of each surface; they are never typed. An item answered by senses (word-sense) names, for each sense, the occurrences it holds for, and together the senses cover every occurrence; the recorder checks them against the data. The interpretation is the observation text, founded in what the evidence shows (basis stated or read, B:131) and tied to its verses (the text names them and does not restate them): the items of every step (S1, 1.1, 1.2, 2.1) state what the dictionary, the verses and the stored structure show of a word and never what a word does for the inner being; their nodes carry the role lexical and no route. The whole file is checked and written in one transaction; any problem refuses all of it. A row answered again withdraws its earlier observations with the reason.

An aspect is recorded as none only where its item allows it (cfg_setting layer.reading none_allowed) and with its reason in words. A group definition and a group's Strong's enrichment are always observed.

A node is on one occurrence (verse_lexical_id) and carries the collection of its surface (a supportive node, the collection of the surface it supports); a node already on the observation for the same occurrence is not written twice, and takes the role. A node with no collection to carry, or on a verse out of scope (B:130), is not written and is listed.

An older observation is deleted as consumed only when live observations carry its meaning: every word occurrence of it is on a live node of a carrier or named as not carried with its reason, the mapping is stated in words (what the old says, which carrier states each part), the traces to it are re-pointed or replaced, and the consumption is kept as `consumed_by`. An observation that holds more than one finding is split first.

An observation that is neither evidence nor inner being contributes nothing to the purposes of the observations (researcher, 2026-11-22): it is commented with its reason and the word occurrences no other live observation holds, then deleted. An observation already marked, or one another observation traces, is not deleted this way.

senses.text: God's thoughts, and the contrast with man's: his thoughts toward his people are many and very deep, the nations do not know the Lord's thoughts, his thoughts are not man's and are as high above them as the heavens, and his thoughts are precious to the psalmist. The thoughts are the Lord's own purposes and mind. Verses: Psa 40:5, Psa 92:5, Psa 139:17, Isa 55:8, Isa 55:9, Mic 4:12.

A question that asks for a hearer's view: 'what do you think?' is put to Simon, to the hearers, to the lawyer, to the chief priests and to those looking for Jesus. It asks the person to give a judgment he already forms. Verses: Mat 17:25, Mat 18:12, Mat 21:28, Mat 22:17, Mat 22:42, Luk 10:36, Joh 11:56.

What seems right or best in someone's eyes: the Hebrew word for eye in the idiom of what appears good to a person, rendered think, think best or thought good. It is a person's own judgment of what is good or fitting. Verses: Num 36:6, 2Sa 10:3, 1Ch 19:3, Jer 40:4, Jer 40:5, 2Sa 3:19.

A thought quoted as inner speech: the Hebrew verb of saying introduces what a person says in himself, and the quoted sentence gives the thought; the Greek of Luk 12:17 does the same with the rich man's words to himself. The thought is inner speech, usually about what others will do or what will follow, and the verse often shows it wrong. Verses: Gen 32:8, 1Sa 27:11, 1Sa 27:12, 2Sa 5:6, 2Ki 7:12, 2Ch 32:1, Neh 6:9, Psa 64:5, 1Sa 20:3, Gen 20:11, Gen 26:9, Gen 31:31, Gen 32:20, Exo 2:14, Jos 22:28, Judg 3:24, Judg 15:2, Rut 4:4, 1Sa 16:6, 1Sa 18:11, 1Sa 18:17, 1Sa 18:21, 1Sa 20:26, 2Sa 14:15, 2Sa 14:17, 2Sa 21:16, 2Ki 5:11, 2Ki 20:19, Job 29:18, Psa 94:18, Isa 39:8, Jer 3:7, Jer 3:19, Eze 20:32, Luk 12:17.

Planning or intending: the Assyrian's heart is set on destroying nations, the prophets intend to make the people forget the name, the Lord plans for his people what they planned, and the one who speaks against God intends to change times and laws. The verbs are of devising and purpose. Verses: Job 6:26, Isa 10:7, Jer 23:27, Dan 7:25, Num 33:56, 1Sa 18:25.

Giving thought to something: calling to mind, reflecting on, attending to, taking thought for or turning the mind to what is named: the psalmist thinks on his ways and on the Lord's rules, the Lord takes thought for the poor, the prudent give thought to their steps, the believer is to think on what is excellent, Jerusalem took no thought of her end. The word is attention of the mind to a matter or person. Verses: Psa 119:52, Psa 119:59, Psa 144:3, Mat 9:4, Eph 3:20, Phili 4:8, Heb 11:15, Psa 40:17, Psa 48:9, Psa 73:16, Pro 14:15, Pro 21:29, Lam 1:9, Jon 1:6.

Reckoning something as so, judging or counting: Paul judges it necessary, a thing is counted unclean by the one who holds it so, the unbelief of Act 26:8 is judged incredible, Judah takes the covered woman for a prostitute, and Job 41:32 counts the deep as white-haired. The word is a judgment that counts or takes something as of a certain kind. Verses: Job 35:2, Job 41:32, 2Cor 12:6, 2Pe 1:13, Rom 14:14, Gen 38:15, Act 26:8, 2Cor 9:5, Phili 2:25.

Being minded: the way a person is set in mind, to rate oneself soberly in Rom 12:3, to hold the same mind or another in Phili 3:15, and the child's mindedness given up in 1Cor 13:11. The Greek verb is of being of a mind or having an attitude. Verses: Rom 12:3, Phili 3:15, 1Cor 13:11.

Thoughts as purposes and devices: the intention of the heart in Gen 6:5, the schemes of the wicked, the thoughts the righteous and the wicked hold, the thoughts to be forsaken, and the wicked thoughts that lodge within. The word is of purpose, plan and device, and the verses place it in the heart. Verses: 1Ch 28:9, Gen 6:5, 1Ch 29:18, Job 21:27, Psa 10:4, Psa 56:5, Psa 94:11, Pro 12:5, Pro 15:26, Isa 55:7, Isa 59:7, Isa 66:18, Jer 4:14, Lam 3:62.

Thoughts as what arises and is held in the mind, known to God or others: they come out of the heart, are perceived by Jesus, are alarmed or answered, are known by the spirit of the person or by the Lord, are shaped by ease, and are led astray. The words are nouns of thought, reasoning and musing, in many Hebrew, Aramaic and Greek words, with the heart or the mind as their place. Verses: Deu 15:9, Job 12:5, Ecc 9:10, Amo 4:13, 2Cor 10:5, Job 20:2, Psa 139:2, Psa 139:23, Ecc 10:20, Eze 38:10, Dan 2:29, Dan 2:30, Dan 4:19, Dan 5:6, Dan 5:10, Dan 7:28, Mat 12:25, Mat 15:19, Mar 7:21, Luk 1:51, Luk 2:35, Luk 5:22, Luk 6:8, Luk 11:17, 1Cor 2:11, 1Cor 3:20, 2Cor 11:3, Heb 4:12, Jam 2:4.

Supposing, holding a belief or imagining something to be so: the belief is stated or put in question, often about oneself or about another, and the verse tests, corrects or reproves it. The hearers think the Gentiles' many words will be heard, that Jesus cannot appeal to his Father, that he came to give peace, that they are wise, stand, or are religious; in the Hebrew verses the speaker is told what the hearer thinks or the Lord says what the house of Israel thinks. The word is a belief held and not yet tested. Verses: 2Sa 18:27, 2Ki 18:20, 2Ch 13:8, Est 4:13, Isa 36:5, Eze 11:5, Mat 5:17, Mat 6:7, Mat 10:34, Mat 26:53, Luk 12:51, Luk 13:2, Luk 13:4, Joh 5:39, Joh 5:45, Joh 16:2, Act 17:29, 1Cor 4:9, 1Cor 7:26, 1Cor 7:40, 1Cor 12:23, 2Cor 11:16, Heb 10:29, 2Cor 12:19, Phili 1:17, Luk 8:18, 1Cor 3:18, 1Cor 7:36, 1Cor 10:12, 1Cor 14:37, Gal 6:3, Phili 3:4, Jam 1:26, Psa 50:21, Mat 20:10, Mar 6:49, Luk 24:37, Joh 11:13, Joh 13:29, Act 8:20, Act 12:9.

Conceiving evil as if in a womb: wicked people conceive trouble, chaff and mischief and give birth to evil, stubble and iniquity. The same verb of conceiving is turned to what a person forms within and brings out in act. Verses: Job 15:35, Isa 33:11, Isa 59:4.

Conceiving a child: the woman becomes pregnant and bears, in the promises and announcements of a son, in the question of the barren, in the cleansed woman who will conceive, in the confession of the psalmist that his mother conceived him in sin, and in the sign of the virgin. The words are Hebrew and Greek verbs and nouns of pregnancy and seed, and the English 'conceive' is bodily. Verses: Num 5:28, Num 11:12, Judg 13:3, Judg 13:5, Judg 13:7, Psa 51:5, Isa 7:14, Mat 1:23, Luk 1:31, Heb 11:11.

'Opinion' in the phrase about not caring for anyone's opinion: the Greek verb is of looking, and the phrase is that Jesus does not look at the person's face, that is, does not weigh people by standing. It is regard for status, not a view held. Verses: Mat 22:16, Mar 12:14.

Opinion as a view that a person holds and declares: Elihu is afraid to declare his opinion and then insists on it, and the fool takes pleasure only in declaring what his heart holds. It is a person's own view, set against understanding. Verses: Job 32:6, Job 32:10, Job 32:17, Pro 18:2.
'Perhaps' as the captain's hope that the god may give a thought to them: the Hebrew particle of possibility, carrying no thinking of its own. Verses: Jon 1:6.
'With no thought of war' as turning back from war: the Hebrew verb is of returning, said of the trusting passers-by who are stripped. It is a turning back, not a thought. Verses: Mic 2:8.
'Well thought of' as a good report: the Greek noun is of testimony, the overseer must have a good report from outsiders. It is how others speak of him, not what he thinks. Verses: 1Ti 3:7.

Thinking as the way the mind works, its understanding or frame: the thinking of people who knew God becomes futile, the believers are to be mature and not children in their thinking, and they are to arm themselves with Christ's way of thinking. It is the mind's mode, with a measure of maturity or futility. Verses: Rom 1:21, 1Cor 14:20, 1Pe 4:1.

older.text: G2168 (thanksgiving withheld) co-occurs with knowledge (M15, G1097), honoring (M22, G1392), reasoning (M63, G1261), foolishness (M16, G0801), and heart (M47, G2588). Here thanksgiving's absence ('did not... give thanks') sits at the hinge of the moral collapse sequence: knowing God but failing to honor or thank Him leads to futile thinking, foolish hearts, and darkness — thanksgiving functions as the withheld response that should have followed true knowledge of God.

Here G2168 appears in a NEGATED clause ('did not... give thanks') — the surface sense is the absence/failure of the act rather than its performance, a notable contrast with John.6.23/1Thess.2.13 where the verb affirms the act. This negative-polarity usage marks Rom.1.21 as the cluster's clearest illustration of the negative pole: thanksgiving withheld as root of idolatrous decline.

G2168 is not itself tagged role-T3 here; the operation-tagged word 'became futile' (G3154, T3) applies to 'their thinking', an internal-state action rather than an interpersonal directed act toward a party.

Since G2168 is the subgroup's sole member strong, the cross-strong comparison this stage exists to perform collapses to a single-strong self-comparison: every occurrence -- whether epistolary-habitual, meal-blessing, exclamatory-nominal, negated, or personal/individual prayer-address -- shares the same root act (a verbal/enacted response of gratitude directed to God, occasionally to a human benefactor as in Rom.16.4) with no second lexeme to diverge from within this subgroup. The genuine internal variation is therefore register/context-driven (liturgical meal-formula vs. epistolary habit vs. individual prayer vs. negated failure) rather than lexical-sense divergence between two different words.

Rom.1.21 is the single occurrence across G2168's full list where the verb is negated ('did not... give thanks'), marking the negative pole of the strong's own range: rather than an enacted response of gratitude, it names the culpable withholding of that response despite prior knowledge of God, standing in structural contrast to every other occurrence (all of which depict thanksgiving actually performed). This is a difference visible only by scanning the strong's complete occurrence list rather than any single-verse reading.

In Rom.1.21 the negated form shows the reverse: the persons 'knew God' (a true perception) yet did not conclude that this knowledge required thanksgiving, revealing a fracture between correct perception and the judgement/response that should follow from it -- knowledge without gratitude, leading to futile thinking.

Across the verses thanksgiving overwhelmingly FOLLOWS a prior belief or perception (of grace given, faith proclaimed, deliverance accomplished, power exercised, prayer answered) -- it is a responsive act rather than a cause of belief. The one negative case (Rom.1.21) shows belief (knowing God) failing to produce the following act of thanks, confirming the normal sequence is belief-then-thanksgiving.

The evidence does not depict thanksgiving itself as a transformation of the person that could be reversible/irreversible; rather it shows a reversible failure-to-respond (Rom.1.21's withheld thanks leading to darkened hearts) alongside an ongoing, renewable practice (habitual thanksgiving) -- so the relevant contrast is presence versus withholding of the act on each occasion, not an irreversible change of state.

Thanksgiving's role reads as belonging to created design (it is the fitting response owed by a creature to its Creator/Benefactor for grace received, and its withholding is portrayed as culpable failure, Rom.1.21) that is now exercised within the fallen condition -- it is both what humanity was designed to render and what fallen humanity characteristically fails to render without renewal (as shown by the contrast between habitual apostolic thanksgiving and the idolaters' withheld thanks).

Thanksgiving is blocked or distorted where knowledge of God is present but not honored (Rom.1.21, leading to futile thinking and darkened hearts), and where it is co-opted for self-congratulation rather than genuine grace-acknowledgment (Luke.18.11's Pharisee). No adversarial-spirit interference is evidenced in these occurrences; the blocking factor shown is internal (pride, willful non-response to known truth).

In Rom.1.21, the person who knows God yet does not give him thanks is shown to have a heart that becomes 'darkened' and thinking that 'became futile' -- the inner-being state where the characteristic's opportunity is present (true knowledge of God) but not taken up is one of foolish, obscured, self-deceived cognition.

The relational scope is broad in principle (any person, believer or outsider, may give thanks, and thanks may be directed to God or to a human benefactor) but the evidence shows it functionally clustered among believers thanking God for one another and, in one negative case, withheld by those who knew God but refused to honor him -- excluding, by that refusal, themselves from the fitting response rather than the characteristic itself excluding any class of person.

The presence of thanksgiving in a person marks a rightly-functioning divine image -- one that perceives grace received and returns acknowledgment; its absence (Rom.1.21, knowing God yet not thanking him) marks the image obscured/darkened, since the capacity for grateful recognition of the Creator is treated as integral to what a rightly-functioning image-bearer does with true knowledge of God.

Thanksgiving, as the fitting creaturely response to God's giving nature, instantiates the aspect of the divine likeness that recognizes and rightly responds to grace/goodness received -- a relational-responsive aspect of the image (rightly ordered gratitude and dependence) rather than an aspect of God's own being shared substantively.

Where thanksgiving is present, it indicates the divine image is functioning rightly with respect to recognizing and honoring God as source of good; where absent despite true knowledge of God (Rom.1.21), it indicates the image is darkened/distorted, evidenced by the futile thinking and foolish heart that follow the withheld thanks.

No occurrence in the evidence depicts thanksgiving itself as a site of direct adversarial (satanic/demonic) attack or interference; the only 'blocking' pattern shown (Rom.1.21) attributes the failure to give thanks to human willful suppression of known truth, not to an adversarial spirit's action.

The pattern of engagement (speech/prayer consistently engaged; cognition/knowledge engaged where present as in Rom.1.21; body occasionally engaged as expressive vehicle, Luke.17.16) indicates thanksgiving's nature as fundamentally a mind-and-mouth response grounded in true perception of a benefactor's action, with the body serving only an expressive, non-essential role -- it is not primarily a bodily or purely emotional faculty-driven characteristic but a cognitive-verbal one.

Thanksgiving is compound in structure: it combines (1) recognition/perception of a favor or grace received, (2) an inward disposition of gratitude, and (3) an outward verbal (or bodily) enactment directed toward the benefactor -- the eu-charis root itself encodes the grace-recognition component fused with the responsive-return component.

The structural opposite of thanksgiving, as shown by its negation in Rom.1.21, is the willful withholding of due acknowledgment despite true knowledge -- ingratitude coupled with a darkened, futile mind; this is the inner-being reality that excludes thanksgiving even where the knowledge that should occasion it is present.

Adjacent characteristics co-occurring with thanksgiving across the verse evidence include: faith (M13, e.g. Rom.1.8, 2Thess.1.3), grace (M50, 1Cor.1.4), love (M51, 2Thess.1.3), prayer/remembrance (M42/M82, Col.1.3, Phil.1.3, 1Thess.1.2, Phlm.1.4, Eph.1.16), knowledge/honoring/heart (M15/M22/M47, Rom.1.21), and building up (M52, 1Cor.14.17) -- these recur frequently, especially the prayer/remembrance pairing in epistolary openings.
